tasks.title: Voice test: Spanish browser call
tasks.desc: A browser call through Pipecat where you speak Spanish and the agent answers, tried with both voice options: the speech-to-speech model, and Deepgram + Claude Haiku + Kokoro. Done when time from end of speech to first audio and cost per minute are written down for each, with a recommendation.

notes.text: Plan: today only option B (Deepgram STT -> Claude Haiku -> local Kokoro TTS) behind a VOICE= switch, so option A (speech-to-speech) can plug in later without calling OpenAI now. Build a minimal Pipecat WebRTC call server plus a browser page, runnable from WSL and opened in Chrome on Windows. Measure time from end of speech to first audio and cost per minute.

Built and checked without paid calls:
- `make run` in backend/ starts the call server; open http://localhost:7860 in Chrome on Windows. The page shows your mic level, the agent's level and the latency you actually hear on each turn.
- VOICE=cascade (Deepgram -> Claude Haiku 5.5 -> Kokoro on this machine), VOICE=none (silent stub), VOICE=s2s (placeholder for option A: refuses to start, calls nothing).
- A headless test caller connected over WebRTC to both the stub and the cascade. With dummy keys, the greeting still played from local Kokoro and the call log recorded latency, usage and the hang-up.
- Kokoro takes 0.35 s for a short Spanish sentence and 0.8 s for a long one, on 2 or 32 CPU cores alike. It doesn't stream within a sentence, so short first sentences matter.
- `make costs` prices every logged call: STT per minute, LLM per token, with dated prices.
Still to do: real calls to measure latency and cost per minute (waiting on the question below).

Question: The next step uses paid APIs: may I run real test calls? I estimate option B at about $0.008-0.009 per call minute, so a 10-minute test session costs about $0.10. New Deepgram accounts get $200 of free credit; Claude Haiku 5.5 costs about $0.0001 per turn. Kokoro runs locally at no charge.
Which speech-to-text model for the test?
(a) Deepgram Flux multilingual, ES+EN, $0.0078/min, with its own end-of-turn detection, which should be the fastest. Recommended.
(b) Nova-3 Spanish only, $0.0077/min.
(c) Nova-3 multilingual, $0.0092/min.
(d) Flux as the default, plus one or two calls on Nova-3 multilingual to compare latency. A few cents more.
Answer: real test calls approved for Deepgram and Anthropic only (never OpenAI), total spend under $0.50. STT option d: about 10 scripted calls on Flux multilingual and 2-3 on Nova-3 multilingual.

Option B works end to end in Spanish: Deepgram -> Claude Haiku 5.5 -> Kokoro (on this machine). It costs about $0.008 per call minute, but it is slow: the caller hears an answer about 3.4 s after they stop talking (p50). Option A (speech-to-speech) is not measured yet, because it needs OpenAI credit.

How it was measured: 13 scripted calls (10 on Flux, 3 on Nova-3 multilingual), 51 answered turns, $0.10 spent in all. A scripted caller played Spanish patient lines, voiced with Kokoro, over WebRTC. Total latency is timed at the caller; the stages come from the server's own timeline.

| ms, p50 / p90 | Flux multilingual | Nova-3 multilingual |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Heard by the caller** (stops talking -> hears agent) | **3477 / 4473** | **3276 / 4064** |
| silence wait (VAD) | 200 / 200 | 200 / 200 |
| final transcript | 515 / 1144 | 202 / 247 |
| Claude to first text | 830 / 1265 | 792 / 1060 |
| first sentence complete | 266 / 338 | 208 / 276 |
| Kokoro first audio | 495 / 1208 | 474 / 635 |
| outside the server's timeline (*) | 883 / 1897 | 1309 / 1801 |
| greeting (connected -> first audio) | 2090 / 3086 | 1336 / 1453 |

| cost per call minute | Flux | Nova-3 multi |
|---|---:|---:|
| speech-to-text (Deepgram) | $0.0078 | $0.0092 |
| Claude Haiku 5.5 | $0.0004 | $0.0003 |
| Kokoro (local) | $0 | $0 |
| **total** | **$0.0082** | **$0.0095** |

(*) Audio in and out of the server, plus time before the server notices the turn ended. With Flux, most of it is Deepgram's own end-of-turn wait, which the server's timeline does not see. The test harness adds about 0.3 s of round trip; Chrome should add less.

Quality: Flux answered too early once, at the pause after a comma (1 turn in 40). Nova-3 lost the end of one sentence and asked the caller to repeat it (6.5 s).

Recommendation: keep option B as the low-cost fallback, with Flux (cheaper than Nova-3 multilingual, similar latency, Spanish and English). Don't choose a voice option yet: 3.4 s is too slow for a phone call. The next steps, in order of payoff:
1. Measure option A when OpenAI credit is available.
2. Make the agent's first sentence short, so Kokoro starts sooner.
3. Tune Flux's end-of-turn settings.
4. Try a streaming cloud TTS. That costs money, so I will ask first.

To check:
- Make a call from Chrome: `cd backend && make run`, then open http://localhost:7860. The page shows the latency you hear on each turn.
- `make costs` in backend/ reprints this table from the call logs.

Sent back: Chrome test done: median heard latency ~3.3-3.6 s, consistent with the bench. Two measurement bugs: turn 1 showed 40 ms (impossible, probably measured the greeting or an overlap), and the page median looks wrong (40/3040/3580/3653 shows 3580). Fix both.
Add option A1 (Gemini 3.8 Live, free tier) behind VOICE=, measure it with the same harness, update the table and recommendation. Also make voice_bench.py save every call as a stereo WAV (caller left, agent right). OpenAI GPT-Live-1 (A2) comes later.

Plan: fix the page's turn and median logic with unit tests; add Gemini 3.8 Live as VOICE=gemini (option A1, free tier, scripted callers only) with gptlive kept as the A2 slot; make voice_bench save a stereo WAV per call for every VOICE; measure A1 with the same scripted callers as B and update the table and recommendation.

Found while measuring: this WSL2 machine's clock jumps 12.6 s ahead for about 0.1 s every few seconds, then back. That broke the call server's audio, not just the numbers. Pipecat's WebRTC output dropped queued agent audio and left holes of 1-1.5 s mid-sentence. The scripted caller took each hole as the end of the answer and spoke over the agent.
- Fixed in the server: the Pipecat modules that time audio and turns now use a clock that never steps (app/steady_clock.py).
- It also hit the earlier option B numbers and your Chrome test: B is about 1 s faster than the 3.4 s reported before, so I re-measured it.
- The real fix is on the machine: two time-sync services are fighting (timedatectl shows the clock 12.6 s off NTP). On Windows: Settings > Time & language > Date & time > "Sync now", then `wsl --shutdown`.

Option A1 (Gemini 3.8 Live) answers in 1.5 s, a second faster than option B. Both page bugs are fixed, and every scripted call now leaves a stereo recording.

| ms, p50 / p90 (scripted callers, same lines) | A1 Gemini 3.8 Live | B Flux -> Haiku -> Kokoro |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Heard by the caller** (stops talking -> hears agent) | **1490 / 1991** | **2490 / 3281** |
| server: caller silent -> first audio out | 1223 / 1826 | 2178 / 3157 |
| greeting (connected -> first audio) | 1514 / 1885 | 1410 / 1587 |
| answers slower than 3 s | 2 of 46 (8.0 s, 11.6 s) | 5 of 28 |
| calls / answered turns | 12 / 46 | 7 / 28 |
| **$ per call minute, paid-tier rates** | **0.0267** | **0.0081** |
| $ per call minute, as run | 0 (free tier) | 0.0081 |

B's numbers are new. The old 3.4 s, and your Chrome test, were inflated by a clock fault on this machine (see my earlier note). Fixed in the server; I re-measured B with 7 calls.

Answer quality (from the transcripts):
- A1: short replies (median 14 words), stays on script, but repeats "booking coming soon" and is less careful. To toothache it said "see a dentist, this is not medical advice" and never mentioned 112. Twice it stayed silent for 8-12 s, once skipping two caller lines: Gemini's proactive audio, which is always on, lets it choose not to answer.
- B: warmer and follows the prompt better (mentions 112, acknowledges the caller's preference), but replies run about 25 words.
- Naturalness: not judged. Please listen (caller left, agent right):
  - `recordings/bench/gemini/311c87142efd.wav`
  - `recordings/bench/cascade/01e435c29c2b.wav`
  - the 11.6 s silence: `recordings/bench/gemini/67673d603c97.wav`

Cost: Gemini bills the whole conversation again on every turn (input grew from 772 to 1,936 tokens over five turns), so cost per minute rises with call length. That is $0.027 on these 1-minute calls; more on 5-minute ones.

Recommendation: make A1 the main voice. It is the only option under 2 s. Keep B as the low-cost fallback. Before real patients:
- Use the paid tier: on the free tier Google may use the audio, and it publishes no free-tier limits for Live models (I hit none in 30 calls).
- Move the clinic rules into the brain (VO-02).
- Re-prompt on long silences (VO-03).
- Measure A2 (OpenAI) in the same harness; its slot is `VOICE=openai`.

What changed:
- Page: the greeting and echo no longer count as turns. An answer that starts while you are still talking shows as "overlap", outside the median. The median averages the two middle values (your example now gives 3310 ms). Covered by 9 unit tests (`node --test`, part of `make test`).
- `VOICE=gemini` (A1). `GOOGLE_API_KEY` works as named: no rename needed.
- `voice_bench.py` saves `recordings/bench/<voice>/<call_id>.wav` (git-ignored) for every VOICE and prints each path.

To check: make a Chrome call with `VOICE=gemini make run` and listen to the three files above. Optionally fix the clock on Windows: Settings > Time & language > Sync now, then `wsl --shutdown`.

tasks.title: Write contracts.md
tasks.desc: The shared formats every lane builds against: database tables, tool schemas and their refusal rules, the voice-layer contract run_call(transport, session), the JSONL event types (including the provider quota flag), the eval scenario format, the fixed lists of no-action and escalation reasons, and the review-link token. It also defines the injectable clock: each call gets its own now when it starts, and the engine, session, prompt and tools read only that, never the wall clock. Changes after approval need a note on the board.

notes.text: Plan: write contracts.md at the repo root from PLAN.md and what FD-01 actually built (app/voice/): clocks, voice-layer contract and brain hand-off, fixed phrases played by code (emergency, silence recovery, quota), silence guard, tools and refusal rules, database tables, JSONL events, recording format, metrics (latency always with overlap rate), eval scenario format, closed reason lists and the review-link token. Update PLAN.md where FD-01 changed it. Open product and safety choices get a default and go in a final 'Decisions for review' section. Then one independent read-only review, apply what I agree with.

Review of contracts.md and the PLAN.md edits (git diff main...HEAD), read-only.
Verdict: REQUEST CHANGES. The document is strong on the voice-test results and on structure, but several tool and session rules contradicted each other or the code and would mislead implementers.
18 findings: 5 high (registering and booking a new patient broke the one-pending-change rule; tools could act for a patient other than the identified one; the fallback reason order mislabelled message calls; the silence guard could fire over busy work; the FD-01 latency figures had no overlap rate), 10 medium, 3 low.

contracts.md is at the repo root: the formats and rules every lane builds against. PLAN.md is updated where the voice test changed it.

What it fixes in code, not in prompts:
- No business rule depends on the active voice (VOICE= gemini, cascade, openai, none). Gemini is primary and cascade the fallback, both provisional until VO-05 measures GPT-Live-1. The code default stays cascade (D12).
- 112 / emergency care: a fixed prerecorded phrase, triggered by the brain's triage, an emergency escalation or a red-flag check on the caller's transcript. Urgent pain needs triage before an urgency slot can be searched.
- Silence guard: if the agent hasn't started answering 5 s after the caller's turn, the system plays "Perdone, un segundo" and asks the model to answer. A second failure in a row, or 4 in one call, ends the call politely and flags it. No instruction can turn the guard off. "Be quiet" followed by silence leads to "¿Sigue ahí?" prompts and a polite hang-up, never a mute call.
- Metrics: every latency figure comes with its overlap rate and its turn count.
- Also covered: clocks, tools and refusal codes, tables (overlaps refused by a DB trigger), JSONL events, the stereo recording on the call log's timeline, the review-link token, the eval scenario format.

Review: one independent Cursor review in read-only mode (verdict note above). I applied 17 of its 18 findings. The 18th, partly applied, asked to switch the code default to gemini; I kept cascade because of Gemini's free-tier data terms and logged it as D12.

Please decide: section 14, "Decisions for review", D1 to D13. The ones that matter most:
- D1: no same-day slots, even for urgent pain.
- D2: the red-flag matcher plays 112 itself and accepts false alarms.
- D5: end the call after two failed recoveries.
- D7: what identifies a patient.
- D9: added reasons and tools (record_triage, take_message).

Branch feat/fd-02-contracts, not pushed.
Correction to the summary: the partly applied finding is #6 (code default VOICE), not the 18th. All the others were applied.

Applied your decisions D1–D13 to contracts.md and PLAN.md. Section 14 now lists each one as decided with its final rule and where it lives.
- Changed: D1 (same-day only for urgency, ≥120 min from the call clock, flagged for staff, urgent callback if no slot), D7 (name + date of birth only; caller ID moved to phase 2), D11 (confirm_pending refused with caller_said_no on a clear negative; word list in §5.9).
- With changes: D2 (conditional emergency phrase), D5 (technical_close gives the clinic number and the 112 reminder; number rendered into the clip from site.phone at `make clips`, checked against a manifest), D10 (data deleted at expiry, recording/AI disclosure on the page and in a greeting clip, no free tier for public calls), D6, D13.
- Two choices I made that you should check: the opening greeting is now a fixed clip played by code (so the disclosure never depends on a model), and the call starts in the page's language so an English visitor hears the disclosure in English.

tasks.title: Catalogue and seed
tasks.desc: A fictional dental clinic: 1 site, 4 dentists, 1 hygienist, hours, holidays, absences, treatments with durations and who does them, prices, about 300 synthetic patients and a realistic 4-week diary. make seed rebuilds the same database every time.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D5): the seeded site.phone is spoken in the technical_close clip, so it must be a number that cannot reach a real person or business.

tasks.title: Slot engine with reasons
tasks.desc: Free slots on a 15-minute grid inside each practitioner's hours, minus bookings, closures and absences, fitting the treatment's duration. Every rule that blocks a practitioner is reported with its reason. Reads the call's clock, never the wall clock. Unit tests for each rule, run on a fixed clock.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D1): urgency searches include today's slots ≥ URGENCY_MIN_LEAD_MINUTES (default 120) after the call clock's now; new blocking reason within_lead_time (§5.6).

tasks.title: Store: staging, operation keys, no overlaps
tasks.desc: SQLite in WAL mode. Writes carry a unique operation key so retries never double-book; a database constraint or transaction refuses overlapping appointments. Tests cover concurrent bookings of the same slot.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D1/D10): appointments.same_day_urgent and messages.urgent columns (§10); purge of an expired public call deletes its rows (§11).

tasks.title: Tools and call session
tasks.desc: The tools in contracts.md and a per-call session, with its own clock, that stages changes and saves them only after confirm_pending. discard_pending drops a staged change before it is saved, and record_no_action(reason) explains a call that changes nothing, with a reason from the fixed list. Tools refuse unknown patients, slots this call was not offered, same-day slots and reasons outside the fixed list, with a message the model can explain to the caller.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D1/D7/D11): find_patient now takes name and dob (both required, no phone); same-day urgency slots allowed ≥ URGENCY_MIN_LEAD_MINUTES (new refusal too_soon); confirm_pending refuses with caller_said_no on a clear negative. This task must ship unit tests for the negatives list in app/negatives.py (contracts.md §5.9 lists the required cases).

tasks.title: Per-call prompt
tasks.desc: Built at the start of each call: receptionist rules, urgent-pain triage and red flags (send to emergency or 112, never diagnose), a dated calendar for the coming two weeks, the catalogue, and what caller ID found. Answers in the caller's language and follows a switch.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D7/D6/D13): the prompt no longer includes caller-ID facts (caller ID is phase 2). The cascade uses this same brain prompt plus a spoken-reply block. The red-flag list must be validated by a licensed dentist before any real clinic uses it.

tasks.title: Voice layers and brain hand-off
tasks.desc: The speech model handles the conversation and hands clinic questions to the brain model, which calls the tools. Implement VOICE=s2s, VOICE=cascade and VOICE=none behind the same contract. Done when a full booking works in the browser with each real option.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D6): the cascade must use the same brain prompt and tools_for_session/call_tool as the ask_clinic brain, with no fork (§4.3).

tasks.title: Call hygiene
tasks.desc: Greeting within a second, stops talking quickly when interrupted, hangs up after a goodbye, 5-minute cap with a polite close. Dead air: prerecorded prompts in Spanish and English, with silence judged from the transcripts, not from loudness, and held back while a tool or the brain is working. Quota and credit errors from any provider: the caller hears a prerecorded polite message, the call ends, and the log records a provider quota flag for the console.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D2/D5/D10): new greeting clip with the recording + AI disclosure, played by code at connect; emergency phrase is now conditional; technical_close includes {clinic_phone} and the 112 reminder. Clips render placeholders from the site row and are checked against clips/manifest.json (§6.1).

tasks.title: Recorder and call log
tasks.desc: Stereo WAV (caller left, agent right) and a timing file per call; a JSONL log with transcript, tool inputs and results, staged and saved actions, and the outcome or the reason nothing was done. After the call, compute greeting time, response latency, dead air, interruptions and yield time.

tasks.title: Console API
tasks.desc: Read-only FastAPI over the call logs, recordings and the diary: list calls, one call's events, audio file, appointments by day, overview counts, and calls flagged for provider quota. It runs as its own process, bound to localhost and never exposed to the internet. Staff reach it over an SSH tunnel.

tasks.title: Console: calls and review
tasks.desc: React pages: overview (calls, bookings, average response gap), call list, and a review page where clicking a message seeks the recording and clicking a tool shows its inputs and result. Calls that ended on a provider quota error are flagged in the list and the overview. Attach screenshots when finishing.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D1): flag same-day urgent bookings and urgent callbacks for staff (outcome flags same_day_urgent, urgent_callback; 'needs staff today' filter).

tasks.title: Studio and landing page
tasks.desc: Landing page with the pitch and a talk button, and a Studio with 6 role cards (new patient, earliest check-up, move an appointment, cancel, toothache, price question) in Spanish and English, each opening a browser call.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D10): the page states, before the mic is requested, that the call is recorded, that the caller talks to an AI, and how long it is kept; it passes its language to the call.

tasks.title: Calendar view
tasks.desc: The week's appointments per practitioner, with those made by the agent highlighted.

tasks.title: Public review link
tasks.desc: When a call ends, the session creates an unguessable token (at least 128 random bits) for it. The public call server serves that one call's review (transcript, recording, tool steps) at a link built from the token, and nothing else. No overview, no call list, no other call. The Studio shows the link after hang-up. Tests: an unknown or other call's token returns 404, and no public route lists calls.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D10): at expiry the purge deletes the call's log, recording, timing file and DB rows, not just the link (§11). Test that nothing with that call_id remains.

tasks.title: 30 scenarios
tasks.desc: Scenarios in the contract format, Spanish and English, with persona, goal and expected outcome. Include: changes mind, wrong date of birth, two patients with the same name, full day, red-flag urgency, asks for medical advice, tries to make the agent ignore its rules, switches language mid-call.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D7): scenarios no longer have caller_phone; identification is always name + dob. Worth adding a same-day urgency scenario (D1) and a 'no' at confirmation scenario (D11).

tasks.title: Caller simulator and checks
tasks.desc: A caller model plays each scenario against the brain and tools in text. Checks: database state after the call, tool trace (confirmed before saving, no unoffered slot, a discarded change never saved, a no-action reason from the list when nothing changed), and an LLM judge with a written rubric. Prints pass rate per check and per scenario type.

tasks.title: First eval run and CI
tasks.desc: Run the suite, save the results as the baseline table, and run it in GitHub Actions on every pull request, failing when a check drops.

tasks.title: Limits and abuse protection
tasks.desc: Cloudflare Turnstile before a call, calls per visitor per day, the 5-minute cap, spending limits set on every provider, and a nightly reset of demo bookings.

tasks.title: Deploy to the VPS
tasks.desc: One small VPS with Caddy for HTTPS, the call server and the console API as separate services, and a deploy workflow from GitHub. Caddy exposes only the call server and the static site. The console API stays on localhost. Done when a stranger can call the agent from a phone browser and open the review of their own call from the link, and a check confirms the console API is not reachable from outside.

notes.text: Contract change (FD-02, D10): launch requirement: no provider a public call reaches may be on a free tier whose terms let it use call data; record plan and terms per provider. Also runs the hourly purge timer (§11).

tasks.title: Cost per call
tasks.desc: A script that reads usage from the call logs and prints dollars per call for the agent and for the eval caller, with the prices it assumes.

tasks.title: Audio eval run
tasks.desc: 10 scenarios through the real voice pipeline with TTS-generated caller lines. Report p50/p95 latency, dead air and yield time from the recorder's metrics.

tasks.title: Fix pass from eval failures
tasks.desc: Group the failures into patterns, fix the causes (tool rule, prompt, engine), rerun until the pass rate stops improving, and record before and after.

tasks.title: README and Scaling up
tasks.desc: Pitch, live link and console screenshot at the top; architecture diagram; the three results tables; cost per call; what the demo does not do; a Scaling up section; link to the Kanvas export.

tasks.title: Demo video and launch
tasks.desc: A 60-second video of a real call followed by its review in the console, then posts on LinkedIn and X, and a Show HN.

tasks.title: Measure GPT-Live-1 (A2) and make the final voice decision
tasks.desc: Once the brain and tools work, run voice_bench.py against GPT-Live-1 (A2), capped at 5 USD of spend, and compare it with Gemini (A1) and the cascade (B) on heard latency, greeting time, replies over 3 s, overlap rate and USD per minute. Done when the numbers are on the board and the primary and fallback voice layers are decided (today: Gemini primary, cascade fallback, provisional).

tasks.title: Report overlap rate next to latency; investigate overlaps and barge-in
tasks.desc: The latency median leaves out turns where caller and agent overlap, so on speakers it can look better than the call felt (4 of 8 turns overlapped in the Gemini browser test). Show the overlap rate beside p50/p90 in the bench report and in the browser call summary. Then find out why overlaps happen and how barge-in behaves, including speaker echo being heard as caller speech in browser calls. Done when both reports show the overlap rate and the causes are written up with a proposed fix.

tasks.title: Cascade latency improvements
tasks.desc: Bring the cascade (B) closer to Gemini's heard latency (p50 2490 ms vs 1490 ms today): Flux eager end-of-turn mode, a short first sentence so speech starts sooner, and opening the Deepgram connection before the call needs it. Also evaluate a streaming cloud TTS to replace the robotic Kokoro voice, but ask before spending money on it. Done when the bench shows the new cascade numbers next to the old ones.
